The Story of Pinyakgandh the Miser

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the bestower of happiness and lord of all the world, and I write the story of Pinyakgandh, who was destroyed by greed for wealth.

Ratnaprabh was king of Kampilya. His queen was Vidyutprabha, beautiful and virtuous. In that city lived a merchant named Jindatt, whose faith in Jain dharma was deep, whose conduct was excellent, and who was honoured in the royal court. There also lived another merchant named Pinyakgandh. He possessed wealth worth many crores, yet the fool was exceedingly greedy and miserly. He never gave a single coin to anyone, nor did he spend his wealth on himself — not on food, drink, or clothing. He had every means of comfort, yet through the ripening of his own sinful karma — or rather, through his own stinginess — he suffered perpetually. His wife was Sundari, and they had a son named Vishnudatt.

One day, while the king's pond was being excavated, a labourer named Udu found an iron chest filled with gold rods. The chest had been buried for thousands of years and was badly corroded by insects and rust. The rods inside were likewise caked with grime, so that their golden nature was not apparent. Udu took one rod and sold it to Jindatt as iron. The merchant bought it, but when he washed it carefully, he discovered it was gold. Deeming it stolen property, he felt it wrong to keep it in his home. Instead, he had a statue of Lord Jina made from it and installed it in the temple with due ceremony. Truly, the righteous fear sin above all else.

Some days later, Udu brought another rod to Jindatt, but this time the merchant refused to buy it, for he knew the wealth belonged to another. Udu then sold it to Pinyakgandh. The miser too realised the rod was gold, but greed overcame him. He told Udu, "If you have more such rods, bring them here. I have great need of iron these days." In this way Pinyakgandh bought some ninety-eight gold rods at the price of iron. Poor Udu did not know their true value and sold them all cheaply.

Thus Pinyakgandh amassed enormous wealth through deceit — yet he neither enjoyed it himself nor gave any of it away. He hoarded it all, living as miserably as before. When death came, he left behind every last coin, unable to take even a single grain of his ill-gotten treasure. Through the heavy sins of greed, deceit, and miserliness, he fell into a lower birth and suffered greatly.

Jindatt, by contrast, used the gold righteously to honour the Lord, and through his lifelong practice of charity and dharma, he progressed on the path to liberation.

This story teaches that wealth without generosity is a curse. The miser who hoards his gold and cheats the innocent gains nothing — he cannot enjoy it in this life, and it drags him into suffering in the next. True wealth is that which is given in charity, for that alone accompanies the soul beyond death.
